**Surah 102: al-Takathur (Rivalry in Worldly Increase)**

The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to call it "the Graveyard," as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Hilal. It is Makki (revealed in Mecca). Abu Hayyan said, "This is the view of all the exegetes (mufassirun)." Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, "According to the most well-known view." What indicates that it is Madani (revealed in Medina), which is the preferred view, is what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Buraydah concerning it. He said: It was revealed concerning two clans of the Ansar, Banu Harithah and Banu al-Harith. They boasted to each other and competed in numbers. One of them said, "Among you is such-and-such and such-and-such?" The others said the same. They boasted about the living, then said, "Come, let us go to the graves." So one of the two groups began to say, "Among you is so-and-so?", pointing to a grave, and "such-and-such", and the other group did likewise. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾, and so on.

Al-Bukhari and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "We used to regard this as part of the Qur'an: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would long for a third valley. Nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust. Then Allah turns in forgiveness towards whoever repents.'" Until it was revealed: ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾, and so on.

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "We continued to doubt the punishment of the grave until ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾ was revealed."

The punishment of the grave is only mentioned in Medina, as in the Sahih (authentic collection) in the story of the Jewish woman. End of quotation. Because the evidence for its being Madani is strong, some eminent scholars said that this is the truth. Its number of verses is eight, by consensus, and it is equal to a thousand verses of the Qur'an.

Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Can none of you manage to recite a thousand verses every day?" They said: "And who can recite a thousand verses?" He said: "Can none of you recite: ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾?"

Al-Khatib in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq and al-Daylami narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a thousand verses in a night will meet Allah, the Exalted, smiling in his face." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who can manage a thousand verses?" So he recited the surah ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾ to its end, then said, peace be upon him: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed equal to a thousand verses."

Ibn al-Mayluq mentioned, regarding the secret of this, that the Qur'an is six thousand and two hundred verses plus a fraction. If we disregard the fraction, a thousand is one-sixth (sudus) of the Qur'an. This surah comprises one-sixth of the Qur'an's objectives. According to what al-Ghazali mentioned, they are six: three principal ones, which are the definition of the one to whom one is called (the Creator), the definition of the Straight Path, and the definition of the state upon returning to Him, Mighty and Majestic; and three complementary ones, which are the description of the conditions of the obedient and the recounting of the statements of the deniers, and the description of the stages of the path, one of which is knowledge of the Hereafter, indicated by the description of the state upon returning to Him, Exalted, which the surah contains. Expressing this meaning with "a thousand verses" is more magnificent and more exalted than expressing it with "a sixth." End of quotation. The matter, and Allah knows best, goes beyond that, and its connection to what precedes it is evident.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate**

﴿Has diverted you﴾: i.e., has preoccupied you. The root meaning of lahw (diversion, heedlessness) is heedlessness. Then it spread to every thing that occupies one, and common usage restricted it to the occupation that gladdens a person, and it is close to play (la'ib). For this reason it occurs in this meaning frequently. Al-Raghib said: lahw is what occupies you from what is important and concerns you. It was said: "That is not the case." Here, the intended meaning of it is heedlessness, and the meaning is: He made you frivolous and heedless.

﴿Rivalry in worldly increase﴾: i.e., competing in multiplicity and boasting about it, such that one group says, "We are more numerous," and the other says, "We are more numerous."

﴿Until you visited the graves﴾. That is, until, when you had exhausted the count of the living, you went out to the graves and moved on to mentioning those buried in them, and so you vied with one another in numbers by counting the dead. The end point is included within what it ends (al-ghayah dakhilah fi al-mughayya), and the occasion of revelation mentioned earlier clarifies this. It is related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that the Banu Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm boasted to see which of them was more numerous. The Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered them, so the Banu Sahm said: "Indeed, transgression destroyed us in the Jahiliyyah." So they counted one another by the living and the dead, and the Banu Sahm outnumbered them. The visiting of graves is, according to what has preceded, taken in its literal sense. As for this view, the phrase is used to express their reaching the mention of the dead, either as a kinayah (metonymy) or as a majaz (figurative usage), and it has been deemed good to take it as a tamthil (allegorical comparison). In al-Kashshaf: he expressed it this way about what was mentioned as a form of mockery directed at them. Some have explained it as though it were said: "You, in this action of yours, are like one who visits graves without a valid purpose." Others explained that visiting graves is for admonition and remembrance of death, but they reversed this and made it a cause of heedlessness, and this is more appropriate. The meaning is: that (rivalry) diverted you, though it does not concern you, nor does it benefit you in your worldly life or your Hereafter, away from what concerns you of the matter of religion, which is more important and more significant than every important matter. The one from whom you are diverted is omitted for the sake of magnification, which is understood from the vagueness produced by the omission, and for the sake of emphasizing the blame, since it indicates that whatever diverts is blameworthy, let alone what diverts from the matter of religion.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is: the rivalry in wealth and children diverted you until you died and were buried, having spent your lives in seeking the world, longing for it, and being consumed by it, until death came to you, and you had no concern except it, instead of what is more fitting for you: striving for your final outcome and working for your Hereafter. Its beginning has been transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Abbas, and it is also transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Abi Shaybah from al-Hasan. On this view, visiting the graves is an expression for death, as the poet said:

"Indeed I have seen al-Dimad as a strange thing: no close friend will be sincere to him for ten years,
Until he tastes al-Dimad, or visits the grave."

And Jarir said:

"Abu Malik visited the graves, so he became the basest of its visitors."

In this there is also an indication of the certainty of resurrection. It is related that a Bedouin heard this and said: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, the people have been raised for the Resurrection, for the visitor departs and does not stay." It is also related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he said: "Whoever visits must return either to Paradise or to Hell." In it there is also an indication of the shortness of the period of staying in the graves. The use of the past tense is either to confirm that it has occurred, or to give precedence to those who died first, or to treat the death of their fathers as equivalent to their own death. Among the things that cause wonder is the statement of Abu Muslim: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with this surah on the Day of Resurrection, rebuking the disbelievers, while at that time they had already visited the graves." It has also been said: this is a rebuke for excessive visiting of graves, out of vying in numbers with those who have passed away, and boasting and competing through them, not for the sake of admonition and remembrance of the Hereafter as is prescribed. The report of Abu Dawud points to this: "I forbade you from visiting graves, so visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter."

It is not hidden that the verse is far from this. Yes, there is no dispute about the blameworthiness of visiting graves for the sake of boasting about the one visited, or for the sake of showing off through the visit, as many ignorant people who ascribe themselves to the Sufis do during their visits to the graves of shaykhs, may Allah have mercy on them. This is in addition to the reprehensible acts they committed there, which they believed to be acts of obedience, and the abominations they adopted as legislation, along with matters too great for the breasts of lines to contain.

Ibn Abbas, Aisha, Mu'awiyah, Abu Imran al-Jawni, Abu Salih, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu al-Jawza', and a group read: "A-lahakum" with a long vowel, in the form of a question. It has been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and also from Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Abi Abla, and al-Kisa'i in one narration, that they read: "A-alhakum" with two hamzahs, and the interrogation is for affirmation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 102, verses 3–4:

﴿Kallā﴾ is a rebuke against occupying oneself with what does not concern one, instead of what does concern one, and a warning about the error in it, because its outcome is grievous.

﴿Sawfa taʿlamūn﴾ (You will come to know) the evil end of what you are engaged in when you witness its consequence. Here al-ʿilm (knowledge) carries the meaning of maʿrifah (cognition), transitive to one object.

﴿Thumma kallā sawfa taʿlamūn﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. Thumma (then) indicates that the second is more emphatic, as a Great One says to His servant: "I tell you, then I tell you: do not do it." It has been said: because the second is more emphatic, it is treated as if it were a different statement and is therefore conjoined (with thumma). Otherwise, an emphatic element is not conjoined to the element it emphasizes, due to the intense connection between them. You should know that the prohibition is the opinion of the linguists, while the exegetes and grammarians have explicitly stated the opposite.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah honour his face, said: The first (warning) is in the graves and the second is at the resurrection, so there is no repetition, the delay (in time) is on its apparent meaning, and there is no problem with the conjunction. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The first rebuke and its threat are for the disbelievers, and what follows is for the believers, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 102, verse 5:

﴿Nay, if you knew with the knowledge of certainty﴾ — that is: if you knew what lies before you with the knowledge of the matter that is certain, i.e., like your knowledge of the matters you are certain of. So the word "knowledge" (ʿilm) is in the genitive construct with its object (idafah ila al-maf'ul), and "certainty" (yaqin) is in the sense of "that which is certain" (mutayaqqan), an adjective of an implied noun. Abu Hayyan permitted that the construction be an idafah of a qualified noun to its adjective, i.e., "the knowledge that is certainty." The benefit of the descriptive term is evident on the basis that knowledge is applied to what is other than certainty. The answer to "law" (lau, "if") is omitted for emphasis of the matter's gravity; i.e., if you knew it thus, you would do what cannot be described or fully comprehended, or it would preoccupy you from competing for abundance and other things, or something similar to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 102, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly you will see the Blazing Fire﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, by which the threat is emphasized, the warning is intensified, and what they were warned of is made clear after being vague, for magnification. It is not permissible for it to be the answer of *law* (lau) of impossibility (al-imtina'iyyah), because it is certain to occur, and the answer of that does not take this form. It was said: it is permissible, and the meaning is: "You will soon know the recompense," then He, glorified is He, said: "If you knew the recompense with the knowledge of certainty now, you would certainly see the Blazing Fire," meaning the Blazing Fire will always be in your sight, never absent from you. And it is as you see.

ثُمَّ لَتَرَوُنَّها ("Then you will surely see it"): this is a repetition for emphasis, and "thumma" (then) indicates greater intensity. It is permissible that the first seeing is when they see it from afar, and the second when they arrive at it or when they enter it; or the first is when they arrive at it and the second when they enter it; or the first is ma'rifah (knowledge) and the second is mushahadah (direct witnessing) and mu'ayanah (ocular observation). It has also been said: it is possible that what is meant is "you will surely see the Hellfire more than once," as an indication of eternal abiding, and this is similar to the dual in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ثُمَّ ارْجِعِ البَصَرَ كَرَّتَيْنِ﴾ ("Then return the gaze twice"). However, this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning.

عَيْنَ اليَقِينِ ("the eye of certainty"): that is, the seeing which is itself certainty, for the disclosure through sight and direct witnessing is above all other disclosures, so it is most worthy of being "the eye of certainty." Thus "ʿayn" here means "itself" (nafs), similar to its use in the phrase: "Zayd came himself." It is an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: the seeing of the eye of certainty. Its governing element is ﴿لَتَرَوُنَّها﴾. It is also permissible that it be an object of contention between the two preceding verbs, and in its unrestricted application there is a discussion which I do not think is hidden from you.

Al-yaqin (certainty) linguistically, according to what al-Sayyid al-Sanad said, is: knowledge about which there is no doubt. Terminologically, it is: believing a thing to be such-and-such, together with believing that it cannot be otherwise than such-and-such, a belief that corresponds to reality and cannot be removed. Al-Raghib said: al-yaqin is a quality of knowledge, above ma'rifah (recognition), diraya (understanding) and their like. It is said: "ilm yaqin" (knowledge of certainty), and one does not say "ma'rifat yaqin." It is the tranquillity of the soul together with the steadfastness of understanding. Al-Sayyid explained yaqin with what you have heard. Several explanations of it have been transmitted from the people of haqiqa (inner realities), namely: ʿilm al-yaqin is the perception of a thing as it is, through what evidence provides; ʿayn al-yaqin is what direct witnessing and unveiling provide; and beyond that is placed haqq al-yaqin. And one of them said, by way of illustration: every intelligent person's knowledge of death is ʿilm al-yaqin; when he witnesses the angels, peace be upon them, it is ʿayn al-yaqin; and when he tastes death, it is haqq al-yaqin. They have other explanations as well. Most of what they have said is based on terminology, so do not be heedless.

Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisa'i read "لَتُرَوُنَّ" with a dammah on the ta'. ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn Kathir in one narration, and ʿAsim likewise, read it with a fatha in "لَتَرَوُنَّ" and a dammah in "لَتُرَوُنَّها". Mujahid, Ashhab and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it with a dammah in both. It is narrated from al-Hasan and Abu ʿAmr, according to one of the two reports from them, that they hamzated the two waws. It is justified on the basis that they found the dammah on the waw burdensome, so they hamzated for lightness, just as they hamzated in "waqt" (time) and "kana" (was)... Analogically, the hamza should not be used, because the dammah is an incidental vowel arising from the meeting of two sukuns, so it is not taken into account. But when it became attached to the word in such a way that it does not disappear, it resembled an original vowel, so they hamzated. They have indeed hamzated from incidental vowels that disappear in pausal position, such as: "ishtaraʾu al-ḍalālah" (they bought error). Thus hamzation in this case is more appropriate.

﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bounty.﴾ It has been said: the address is to the disbelievers. This is related from al-Hasan and Muqatil, and al-Tibi (al-Tibi, the commentator) chose it.

"Al-Na'im" (the bounty) is general, covering everything one enjoys: food, drink, bedding, and mounts. The same is said of the earlier addresses.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he stated that the address in ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ is to the polytheists. They understood "seeing" to mean seeing the entering of it. They also understood the questioning here as a questioning of rebuke and reproach, because they did not believe in Him, exalted and majestic. It has been said that the questioning may take place [p. 226] after seeing the Fire and entering it, as they are questioned about other things in the same way, as indicated by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Every time a group is thrown into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did no warner come to you?"﴾ and His saying, glorified be He: ﴿What led you into Saqar?﴾ This is because at that time it is more painful and more likely to bring them to confess their shortcoming. So "thumma" (then) is on its literal sense. It may also be at the place of reckoning before entering, and then "thumma" indicates sequence in mention.

It has also been said: the address is restricted to everyone whose worldly life has distracted him from his religion, and the bounty is restricted to what has preoccupied him from that. This is because it is evident that the address in ﴿Competition in worldly increase has distracted you﴾ and so on is to those who are distracted. This serves as an indicator of what has been mentioned, and it is supported by many texts such as His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah?"﴾ and ﴿Eat of the good things﴾. This also takes the questioning to be a questioning of rebuke, and it includes the disbelievers and the sinful believers.

It has also been said: the address is general, and so is the questioning, which encompasses the questioning of rebuke and other kinds. The bounty is specific, and there are various opinions about it.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in his Zawa'id al-Zuhd (Additions to the Book of Asceticism), reported from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet: "It is security and health."

Al-Bayhaqi reported from the Amir 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "The bounty is well-being."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu al-Darda', traced to the Prophet: "Eating wheat bread, sleeping in the shade, and drinking the water of the Euphrates cooled."

Ibn Jarir reported from Thabit al-Bunani, traced to the Prophet: "The bounty that one will be asked about on the Day of Resurrection is a morsel that sustains him, water that quenches him, and a garment that covers him."

al-Khatib reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explain it. He said: 'Dates, water, and cracked bread (fala al-kisar).'"

It is related from him and from Jabir that it is the sufficiency of food and drink. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is the lightening of the laws and the facilitation of the Qur'an.

It is reported from Jabir al-Ju'fi, of the Imamiyya, who said: "I entered upon al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: 'What do the people of ta'wil (interpretation) say about His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bounty﴾?' I said: 'They say: the shade and cold water.' He said: 'If you were to bring someone into your house, seat him in shade, and give him water, would you hold it over him?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'Allah, exalted be He, is too noble to feed His servant and give him drink and then ask him about it.' I said: 'What is its ta'wil?' He said: 'The bounty is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah, exalted be He, blessed the people of the world through him and rescued them by him from misguidance. Have you not heard His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah certainly conferred favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger﴾?'"

And from the narration of al-'Ayyashi, also of the Imamiyya, that Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding the verse: "What is the bounty in your view, O Nu'man?" He said: "Sustenance of food and cold water." Abu 'Abd Allah said: "If Allah were to stop you before Him to ask you about every meal you ate or drink you drank, your standing before Him would surely be long." Abu Hanifa said: "Then what is the bounty?" He said: "We, the People of the House, are the bounty. Allah, exalted be He, blessed the servants through us, and through us they were united after they had been divided, and through us Allah, exalted be He, joined their hearts and made them brothers after they had been enemies, and through us He guided them to Islam, which is the bounty that does not end. Allah, exalted be He, will ask them about the true right of the bounty which He, glorified be He, bestowed upon them, and it is Muhammad and his family, upon him and upon them be prayers and peace."

Both reports, in my view, have no soundness, and there is in them what cries out against their authenticity, as is not hidden from one who listens attentively while being a witness. The truth is that the address and the bounty are general. However, the believer is not reproached for anything he received in this world; rather, he is questioned without being reproached. Reproach is directed only at the disbeliever, as stated in a hadith narrated by al-Tabarani from Ibn Mas'ud.

The generality of the address is indicated by what Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others reported from Abu Hurayra who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out one day and found Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. He said: 'What brought you out of your houses at this hour?' They said: 'Hunger, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, what brought you out is what has brought me out. Stand up.' They stood up with him, peace be upon him, and he came to a man of the Ansar, but he was not in his house. When the woman saw the Prophet (ﷺ) she said: 'Welcome.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Where is so-and-so?' She said: 'He has gone to fetch sweet water for us.' Then the Ansari came and looked at the Prophet (ﷺ) and his two companions and said:

'Praise be to Allah, there is no one today more generous to guests than me.' So he went and brought a cluster of dates containing unripe and ripe dates, and said: 'Eat of this.' He took a knife, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Beware of the milk-giver.' So he slaughtered for them, and they ate of the sheep and of that cluster and drank. When they were satisfied and quenched, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr and 'Umar: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will surely be asked about this bounty on the Day of Resurrection.'"

In the narration of Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and his two companions went to the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. His wife said: 'Welcome to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and whoever is with him.' Abu Ayyub came and cut a cluster. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I did not intend that you cut this for us; why did you not pick from its dates?' He said: 'I loved, O Messenger of Allah, that you eat from its dates, its unripe dates, and its ripe dates.' Then he slaughtered a young goat, roasted half of it and cooked half of it. When it was placed before the Prophet (ﷺ), he took some of the goat and placed it on a loaf of bread, and said: 'O Abu Ayyub, take this to Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, for she has not had anything like this for days.' Abu Ayyub took it to Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her. When they had eaten and were satisfied, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Bread, meat, dates, unripe dates, and ripe dates.' His eyes shed tears, peace be upon him. Then he said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, this is indeed the bounty you will be asked about. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bounty.﴾ This is the bounty you will be asked about on the Day of Resurrection.'" This was hard on his companions, so the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Yes. When you find something like this, strike with your hands, and say: 'In the name of Allah.' When you are satisfied, say: 'Praise be to Allah who fed us, blessed us, and bestowed favor upon us; for this is sufficient in exchange for that.'"

The intent in this report is not to restrict the bounty absolutely to what has been mentioned. Rather, the restriction is in relation to that time when they were hungry. Likewise with what is soundly reported with limitation to one or two things or more. All of that is by way of example, with some individual instances singled out for mention due to a matter the circumstance required. This is supported by his saying, peace be upon him, in another narration, when mentioning some of these things: "This is among the bounty you will be asked about," with "min" (among) being partitive. In al-Tafsir al-Kabir (The Great Commentary) it says: the truth is that the questioning encompasses the believer and the disbeliever about all bounties, whether they are indispensable or not. This is because everything Allah, exalted be He, grants must be spent in His obedience, glorified be He, and not in disobedience, exalted and majestic be He. Thus the questioning is about everything. This is confirmed by his saying, peace be upon him: "The feet of a servant will not move until he is asked about four things: about his life, how he spent it; about his youth, how he wore it out; about his wealth, from where he earned it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, what he did with it."

For every bounty falls within what he, peace be upon him, mentioned. It is problematic in light of what 'Abd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad reported in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and al-Daylami reported from al-Hasan, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Three things for which the servant will not be held accountable: the shade of a hut under which he shelters, a morsel with which he sustains his back, and a garment with which he covers his nakedness.'"

It has been answered that if it is sound, the meaning is that he will not be scrutinized in reckoning regarding them. It has also been said: the meaning is what the servant is compelled to need of these for his life. So reflect. I have seen in some books that the food eaten with an orphan is not asked about, because eating with him is a consolation to his heart and a removal of his loneliness, so it is like thanks, and he is not questioned about it with a questioning of rebuke. There is some doubt about the soundness of this. And Allah knows best.
